albums.album: The Incredible Jazz Guitar of Wes Montgomery
albums.blurb: Montgomery's second Riverside album, cut in two January 1960 sessions in New York with pianist Tommy Flanagan and the Heath brothers on bass and drums. It's the record that introduced his self-taught signatures — thumb-picked lines and melodies doubled in octaves — to a national audience, and it contains two of his most durable originals, "Four on Six" and "West Coast Blues." An entirely instrumental quartet date, split between those originals and standards like "Polka Dots and Moonbeams."
albums.reception: The album was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999 and selected for the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry in 2017.

albums.blurb: The debut that precedes the polished disco-pop of Discovery: sixteen tracks of raw, loop-driven house, acid, and funk, largely recorded in Thomas Bangalter's bedroom studio in Paris and released on Virgin in January 1997. "Da Funk" and "Around the World" were the singles that carried the so-called French touch sound out of the Paris club scene and onto international radio and MTV.
albums.reception: Homework peaked at number 3 in France and number 8 on the UK Albums Chart, was certified Gold in the US in 2001, and had sold more than two million copies worldwide by February 2001.

albums.blurb: Bush's fifth album, written and self-produced in the 48-track studio she built behind her family's farmhouse after leaving the London studio system. It splits in two: a first side of standalone songs built on the Fairlight CMI sampler ("Running Up That Hill," "Cloudbusting") and a second-side song suite, "The Ninth Wave," about a woman adrift at sea overnight. It marked her commercial resurgence after the dense, low-selling 1982 album The Dreaming.
albums.reception: The album entered the UK Albums Chart at number one and spent three weeks on top, and "Running Up That Hill" reached number 3 in 1985 before returning to hit number one in the UK in 2022.
